## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways based on statistical significance, biological coherence, and likely relevance to kidney disease. Notably, inflammatory and innate immune pathways are among the strongest signals, particularly neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695, p = 2.88 × 10−16, associated protein count = 89) and the nuclear factor kappa B transcription factor motif (TF:M00194_1, p = 1.49 × 10−3, associated protein count = 44), suggesting that persistent inflammatory activation is a central feature of disease biology. This is consistent with extensive literature showing that nuclear factor kappa B signaling promotes cytokine production, leukocyte recruitment, and tissue injury in chronic and acute kidney disorders, while neutrophil granule release contributes to oxidative stress, endothelial damage, and amplification of renal inflammation.

Furthermore, pathways related to extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue injury are strongly enriched, including degradation of the extracellular matrix (REAC:R-HSA-1474228, p = 1.11 × 10−13, associated protein count = 41) and matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129, p = 4.07 × 10−6, associated protein count = 13). These findings are highly relevant because abnormal extracellular matrix turnover is a hallmark of kidney disease progression, linking inflammatory injury to glomerular and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Supporting this interpretation, enrichment of actin-based cell projection (GO:0098858, p = 2.97 × 10−2, associated protein count = 17) and late endosome (GO:0005770, p = 4.55 × 10−2, associated protein count = 24) points to altered cytoskeletal organization and vesicular trafficking, processes that are essential for podocyte structure, tubular transport, and protein handling in the kidney.

In addition, several metabolic and molecular function terms indicate disturbances in lipid and ion handling, including carboxylic acid binding (GO:0031406, p = 1.94 × 10−8, associated protein count = 30), calcium ion binding (GO:0005509, p = 7.27 × 10−11, associated protein count = 56), phosphatidylcholine metabolic process (GO:0046470, p = 5.70 × 10−4, associated protein count = 13), and fatty acid transport (GO:0015908, p = 4.18 × 10−4, associated protein count = 16). These signals fit well with published studies showing that calcium dysregulation, lipid metabolic stress, and altered fatty acid handling contribute to tubular cell injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive fibrosis. Finally, disease-oriented enrichments such as rheumatoid arthritis (KEGG:05323, p = 6.08 × 10−8, associated protein count = 25), malaria (KEGG:05144, p = 1.15 × 10−7, associated protein count = 18), amyloidosis (HP:0011034, p = 2.82 × 10−2, associated protein count = 12), and acute ischemic stroke (HP:0002140, p = 3.55 × 10−2, associated protein count = 10) likely reflect shared mechanisms of systemic inflammation, vascular injury, and protein deposition that are also relevant to renal pathology. Overall, the most significant pathways converge on inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, cytoskeletal and endosomal dysfunction, and metabolic stress, all of which are well-supported drivers of kidney injury and progression in the literature.
